paragraphs.heading: A telescope built on a lens
paragraphs.text: A refracting telescope, or refractor, is an optical telescope that forms its image with a lens, called the objective. The usual layout puts that lens at the front, a long tube behind it, and an eyepiece or instrument at the back, where the view comes to focus. Refractors were the earliest kind of optical telescope. The design was once used in spyglasses and astronomical telescopes, and it still turns up in long-focus camera lenses.

paragraphs.heading: How the lens does its job
paragraphs.text: Every refractor works on the same idea. The objective bends, or refracts, incoming light, so rays that arrive parallel meet at a focal point. Paired with an eyepiece, the lens gathers more light than a bare eye can, brings it to a focus, and shows the viewer an image that is brighter, clearer and larger. How much a refractor magnifies is a simple division: the focal length of the objective over the focal length of the eyepiece.

paragraphs.heading: Galileo's version
paragraphs.text: The first record of a refractor comes from the Netherlands around 1608, when Hans Lippershey, a spectacle maker from Middelburg, tried and failed to patent one. Galileo Galilei heard of it in Venice in May 1609, built his own, and used it to make astronomical discoveries. His design paired a converging front lens with a diverging eyepiece and gave an upright image. Poor lenses forced him to shrink the opening of the objective, so the view was blurry, distorted and narrow, yet his strongest instrument still magnified about 30 times. With it he saw craters on the Moon, Jupiter's four largest moons and the phases of Venus.

paragraphs.heading: Kepler's improvement
paragraphs.text: In 1611 Johannes Kepler improved on Galileo's design by using a convex eyepiece in place of the concave one. His layout gave a much wider field of view and could reach far higher magnifications, but it showed the image upside down. Its objective was still a single simple lens, so it needed a very high focal ratio to limit aberrations. That pushed builders toward huge instruments: Johannes Hevelius made one with a 46-metre focal length.

paragraphs.heading: Fixing the colour problem
paragraphs.text: The next big step was the achromatic lens, an objective made of more than one piece of glass. Chester Moore Hall invented it in 1733, and John Dollond invented and patented it on his own around 1758. It joins two kinds of glass with different dispersion, crown and flint, which cuts chromatic and spherical aberration and brings two wavelengths, usually red and blue, to focus in the same plane. Telescopes no longer had to be so long, and Dollond's achromats became popular in the 18th century. Trouble with glassmaking, though, kept these objectives to about 10 cm across.

paragraphs.heading: Why reflectors took over
paragraphs.text: In the later 1800s, large refractors enjoyed great popularity. For most research, though, they have since given way to reflecting telescopes, which allow larger apertures. The ideas behind refractors live on in other optical devices, such as binoculars and zoom or telephoto lenses.
